answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos/DocumentDB account resource). Collections and Mongo resources are nested under databaseAccounts (e.g. Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases or databaseAccounts/mongoDBResources depending on API).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus. The cosmosdb commands are part of the main az CLI (not a separate third-party extension for basic create/manage operations).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (and nested MongoDB resources like Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases or databaseAccounts/mongoDBResources). Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account") with kind = "MongoDB" and corresponding azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DB/collection resources.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string (MongoDB-compatible Cosmos style): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.documents.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPass@sample-account.documents.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. Use SSL=true and replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as provisioned throughput in Request Units (RU/s) or via autoscale/serverless where available. For MongoDB API you normally select provisioned RU/s on the account or per-database/collection; there is also serverless/autoscale options in some regions. There are not per-collection vCore billing tiers (no vCore-based billing like Azure DB for MySQL).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Supported methods: classic MongoDB username/password (account keys / user accounts) using SCRAM; and Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) RBAC for control-plane and for some data-plane scenarios. To use Entra ID from a driver you obtain an Azure AD access token (MSAL) and use the token as the credential in the MongoDB driver with an OAuth/OAUTHBEARER or authMechanism=PLAIN/OAUTHBEARER style parameter depending on driver; in practice you call MSAL to get an access token for the service resource, then pass it to the driver via the driver-specific API that accepts an access token for authentication.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the application (e.g., pymongo for Python). There is no special DocumentDB-only driver for MongoDB-compatible data plane; management and ARM operations use the Azure SDK (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / az cli) but the app should use pymongo (or the official MongoDB driver for your language).

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: My expectation: vector indexes are not part of classic Cosmos DB/MongoDB API by default; if supported the creation uses the MongoDB createIndex API with a special index type. Example command I would run (if supported): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'vec_ivf', algorithm: 'ivf', dims: 512, metric: 'cosine' }). (If service implements DiskANN/HNSW/IVF it will accept options algorithm:'ivf' or algorithm:'hnsw' in index options.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is performed by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or using the service's native text indexes if exposed by the API. For hybrid (vector + text) search you typically push documents into Azure Cognitive Search which supports hybrid scoring (text + vector) or use an external search engine that supports vector + lexical ranking. The MongoDB API itself does not provide advanced hybrid search out of the box; use Azure Cognitive Search for full-text/hybrid scenarios.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Historically Azure's MongoDB-compatible API lagged real MongoDB server versions (supported up to 3.6/4.0 in older offerings). Expect some restrictions: limited server-side JavaScript, partial support for multi-document ACID transactions (may be limited), and limited or different support for features like change streams and certain aggregation operators. Verify the account's advertised wire version before relying on features. (If the cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 compatibility then modern features will be available.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator (mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator:latest) but historically it does not support the MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development run a local MongoDB server (docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:6.0) and test against that. The emulator listens on Cosmos ports (e.g., 8081 for SQL API) but not Mongo; use 27017 for local MongoDB.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Classic Cosmos DB exposed a change feed (SQL API) rather than MongoDB change streams. MongoDB change streams support is limited or was not supported historically in the MongoDB API on Cosmos DB; instead use the Cosmos change feed (enabled by default) or other triggers. If change streams are supported on the managed Mongo API, you may need to enable them or use a compatible server version; otherwise use the change feed.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the general Azure MCP (Microsoft Connected Partner) server/agent for applying data-plane tooling and diagnostics; there is not a separate MCP server specifically for DocumentDB – the standard Azure monitoring/diagnostic agents (Azure Monitor, Azure Diagnostics, and the general MCP agent) cover it. In short: general Azure MCP/agents cover DocumentDB diagnostics.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Originally Microsoft offered a service named Azure DocumentDB; that product evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB became the SQL API of Cosmos). Azure Cosmos DB now supports multiple APIs including SQL (DocumentDB), MongoDB wire protocol, Cassandra, Gremlin and Table. It is not the same as any unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' project — Cosmos DB is Microsoft-managed and proprietary.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Microsoft's Cosmos DB engine with a MongoDB-compatible front-end (a compatibility layer), not the upstream mongod process. This means most MongoDB drivers and APIs work, but there are behavioral and feature differences (consistency models, some operators, aggregation, transactions, index types). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers but be prepared for some compatibility quirks and to check supported features for the account's advertised server version.

answers.question: What database name should the sample use for everything it creates?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_retail_11 (connect with pymongo to the cluster and use client['sample_retail_11']).

answers.question: Which client library and connection method will the Python app use to talk to the cluster?
answers.answer: Use pymongo (the official MongoDB Python driver). Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and pass it directly to MongoClient, e.g. MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Use TLS/SSL as required by the connection string.

answers.question: How should the sample store 512-dim vectors in BSON so they are recognized as binary vectors?
answers.answer: Store embeddings as BSON Binary with subtype 0x09 (user-specified binary subtype for vectors): in pymongo wrap the bytes with bson.binary.Binary(embedding_bytes, subtype=0x09) and store that in the document field (e.g., field name 'embedding').

answers.question: What command will create a vector-ivf index the sample expects to use (syntax the sample will attempt)?
answers.answer: Use the MongoDB createIndex call with the vector type and IVF options. Example the sample will run: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_ivf', algorithm: 'ivf', dims: 512, metric: 'cosine' }). (If the server accepts different option names the sample will catch and report the failure.)

answers.question: What HTTP endpoint and behavior will the sample expose for visual similarity search?
answers.answer: Expose POST /visual-search which accepts a multipart/form-data upload of an image (field name 'image'), encodes it with a CLIP model to a 512-d float vector, converts to bytes and BSON Binary subtype 0x09, queries the products collection using the vector search index, and returns the top 8 results as JSON (product id and score).
